content: Hello, I’m GPTREI, your requirements elicitation assistant. I’ll be gathering detailed information about the VII Data Use Analysis and Processing System to make sure we understand the needs clearly and capture the right requirements. Before we begin, are you aligned with this interview scope, or do you have different expectations for what we should cover?

Yes, I’m aligned with that scope. We’re looking at a prototype that can bring together connected-vehicle and related transportation data, process it, and turn it into outputs useful for safety, traffic operations, asset management, winter operations, and planning. I’m expecting us to focus on what data comes in, how it gets consolidated and transformed, and how the results are shared with agencies and, where appropriate, the public.
To start off, could you please introduce yourself and your connection to this project?

I’m representing the Michigan Department of Transportation’s perspective on this prototype effort. My role is to make sure the system supports our operational and planning needs and that it can realistically handle the kind of data we expect from connected vehicles and other sources.
Thank you. Could you describe the current process or systems you use today for collecting, consolidating, and using these transportation data sources?

Right now, those data sources are pretty fragmented. Vehicle, traffic, weather, and traveler information come in from different systems and vendors, and a lot of the consolidation is done manually or through separate tools that don’t always talk to each other well. In practice, that means it takes time to clean, line up, and interpret the data before it can be used for operations or planning.
What current processes do you want to change or improve, or what main features do you hope to get from this prototype?

We want to reduce the manual work and get to useful information much faster. Ideally, the prototype would automatically ingest the incoming data, standardize it enough to compare and combine sources, and produce outputs that are easy for our staff and partner agencies to use. We’re also hoping it can show us which kinds of connected-vehicle data are actually valuable for different use cases before we invest in something larger.
Based on your description, do you think the prototype should also include a way to evaluate or score which data sources are most useful for each use case?

Yes, that would be very helpful. We’d want some way to see which sources perform well for safety, winter operations, traffic management, and planning, because not every data feed will be equally useful for every purpose. Even a simple scoring or comparison view would help us decide what to rely on and what to deprioritize.
Are there any other main features you’d like to see in this prototype, perhaps something we haven’t focused on yet?

I’d want basic visualization and reporting so people can actually understand the outputs without digging into raw data. It would also be useful if the system could flag data quality issues or gaps, because that will affect trust in the results. Beyond that, I think the main thing is keeping it flexible enough to support multiple use cases without being overly complicated.

So far, I have these main features: automated ingestion, data standardization and consolidation, outputs for staff and partner agencies, evaluation of source usefulness by use case, basic visualization and reporting, and data quality/gap flagging. Is that an accurate summary?

Yes, that sounds accurate to me. I’d just add that the prototype should help us see the information in a way that supports both operational decisions and longer-term planning, not just one or the other. Other than that, your summary captures what we need pretty well.
Which of these features is the highest priority for the prototype?

The highest priority is automated ingestion and consolidation, because without that we can’t really test the rest of the concept. Right after that, I’d put the ability to evaluate usefulness by use case, since the prototype is really about learning what data is worth keeping and applying.
After those, which feature should come next in priority?
After that, I’d put data quality and gap flagging next. If we can’t tell whether the incoming data is incomplete or unreliable, then the outputs and evaluations won’t be very trustworthy.
And after data quality and gap flagging, which feature would you prioritize next?

I’d say basic visualization and reporting would come next. That’s what will let staff and partners actually see the results and make sense of the consolidated data without having to work through raw feeds.

We want it to continuously bring in the main streams we expect to have available, like connected vehicle data, traffic conditions, weather, and traveler information. The prototype should line those up into a common structure so we can compare and combine them by location and time, rather than treating each feed separately. Ideally it would also preserve enough detail to trace outputs back to the original source if we need to check how something was derived.
Could you describe the current system or process you use today for ingesting and consolidating those data sources, if any?

There isn’t really a unified system today. In practice, different teams or partners tend to get their own feeds and work with them separately, and a lot of the consolidation happens manually or in ad hoc analysis when someone needs a specific answer. That makes it hard to reuse the data consistently across use cases.
Please elaborate on what you want the usefulness-by-use-case evaluation to accomplish, and what “useful” should mean for your team.

We want the system to help us judge whether a given data source actually supports a specific need, like incident response, winter maintenance, corridor operations, or planning. “Useful” would mean it is timely enough, accurate enough, covers the right geography or roadway, and is available consistently enough to be trusted for that use. If a source only works for some scenarios or has gaps, we still want that captured clearly rather than treating it as fully reliable.
Could you describe the current process or tools you use today to judge whether a data source is timely, accurate, and consistent enough for a given use case?

Mostly it’s a mix of staff judgment, side-by-side review with other known data, and occasional manual checks in spreadsheets or simple analysis tools. There isn’t a formal scoring process that everyone uses the same way, so the assessment can vary depending on who is looking at it and what the immediate need is.
Please elaborate on what you want data quality and gap flagging to accomplish, including what kinds of issues the system should detect.

We want it to automatically catch obvious problems like missing records, delayed feeds, duplicate messages, inconsistent timestamps, and values that look out of range or don’t line up with nearby data. It should also flag coverage gaps, so if a corridor or time period isn’t represented well, we know that right away. The goal is not to reject everything, but to give us a clear warning about where the data may be weak or incomplete.
Could you describe the current process or tools you use today for identifying missing records, delayed feeds, duplicates, or coverage gaps?

Right now that’s mostly done after the fact, when someone notices something looks off in a report or an analysis. People may run manual checks, compare against another source, or look for obvious holes in the data, but it’s not standardized and it can take a while to catch issues. We don’t have a single tool doing that continuously across all feeds.
Please elaborate on what you want basic visualization and reporting to accomplish, and who needs to use those outputs.

We want straightforward views and reports that help people quickly understand what data came in, what was flagged, and whether it looks usable for the intended purpose. The outputs need to work for internal analysts and transportation staff first, but we also expect some higher-level summaries could be shared with managers or the public depending on the use case. It does not need to be highly polished at this stage, but it should be easy to interpret and practical for decision-making.
Who else do you think has valuable insights into the project and whose needs should be considered, and why?

Our internal operations people, traffic analysts, asset management staff, winter operations folks, and planning staff all have useful perspectives because they each care about different data qualities and outputs. We should also consider IT and data governance folks since they’ll have opinions on integration, security, and how data gets stored and shared. If we include external partners or vendors, they may help explain what data is realistically available and how often it can be provided.
What would success look like for this prototype from MDOT’s perspective?

Success would mean we can show, with real or representative data, that the system can bring multiple feeds together and tell us whether they are good enough for a few important use cases. If the prototype can clearly flag quality issues, show useful summaries, and help staff make a faster judgment than they do today, that would be a strong result. We’d also want it to be credible enough that people can see how it could grow into something operational later.

To summarize, we discussed: automated ingestion and consolidation of connected vehicle, traffic, weather, and traveler data; evaluating usefulness by use case; data quality and gap flagging; basic visualization and reporting; preserving traceability to original sources; and supporting both operational and planning decisions. Is there anything else you would like to add?

One thing I’d add is that the prototype should be flexible enough to handle data sources changing over time, because feeds and formats won’t stay stable. It would also help if we can document assumptions and known limitations clearly, so users understand what the system can and cannot conclude from the data. Beyond that, I think the main pieces are covered.

Thank you for your valuable insights. We will follow up with any additional questions or clarifications needed. Based on our discussion, I will prepare a detailed summary and share it with you for review.
That sounds good. I’m happy to review the summary and clarify anything that needs tightening up.
